title: Network Interface & Routing Configuration
markdown:
# Network Interface & Routing Configuration

Before any process can send or receive data across a network, the operating system needs to know three things: which physical or virtual device to use, what address to assign to that device, and where to send packets that are not destined for the local subnet. The `ip` command controls all three — replacing the older `ifconfig` and `route` utilities that you may still encounter in legacy scripts and tutorials.

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/7549ac1f4b11cc59ba30c571a184bc22b28fce46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2015/images/linux-network.svg)

The `ip` command is part of the `iproute2` package and organises its functionality into **objects**: `link` manages interface state and properties, `addr` manages IP addresses, `route` manages routing tables, and `neigh` manages the ARP cache. Each object follows the same verb pattern: `ip <object> <verb> [arguments]`. Once you understand the pattern for one object, the rest follow naturally.

By the end of this lab, you will be able to:

- List network interfaces and their addresses with `ip link show` and `ip addr show`
- Bring interfaces up and down with `ip link set`
- Add and remove IP addresses on an interface with `ip addr add` and `ip addr del`
- Inspect and modify the routing table with `ip route show`, `ip route add`, and `ip route del`
- Use `ip route get` to trace which route the kernel will use for a given destination
- Use network namespaces to safely practise interface configuration without risking your SSH connection

## The Scenario: Configuring a New Application Server

A new VM — **app-01** — has been provisioned in the `Poridhi.io` infrastructure. It booted with only a loopback interface configured. Before it can serve HTTP traffic and communicate with the database cluster on the `10.20.0.0/24` subnet, three things need to happen:

1. The primary network interface must be confirmed as `UP`
2. A secondary IP address must be added for the staging environment
3. A static route to the database subnet must be configured through the correct gateway

| What | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `veth-ns` | Virtual interface inside the namespace — represents app-01's primary NIC |
| `veth-host` | The host end of the virtual cable — acts as the next-hop from the namespace's perspective |
| `10.10.0.100/24` | Primary IP assigned to `veth-ns` — app-01's production address |
| `10.10.0.200/24` | Secondary IP assigned to `veth-ns` — the staging environment alias |
| `10.20.0.0/24` | Simulated database subnet — not directly connected, reachable via a static route |
| `10.10.0.1` | IP assigned to `veth-host` — acts as app-01's next-hop gateway within this lab setup |

All `ip` command changes are **non-persistent** — they exist only in memory and are automatically lost when the VM reboots. On Ubuntu, making network changes survive a reboot requires editing Netplan configuration files under `/etc/netplan/`, which is outside the scope of this lab. Here we focus entirely on runtime configuration using the `ip` command.

We will practise using a **network namespace** — a Linux kernel feature that creates an isolated network stack with its own interfaces, addresses, and routing table — rather than modifying your VM's primary interface directly. The reason is simple: if you accidentally bring down the interface your SSH session is running over, the connection drops immediately and the only recovery is a VM restart. The namespace gives you a safe sandbox where every operation is fully reversible without touching the live interface.

## Part 1: Understanding Network Interfaces

A **network interface** is the kernel's representation of a network device. It can be physical (a real NIC) or virtual (a loopback, a bridge, a tunnel, or a veth pair). Each interface has:

- A **name** (`eth0`, `lo`, `ens3`, `enp0s3` — the exact format depends on the naming scheme)
- A **state** (`UP` or `DOWN`)
- One or more **IP addresses** bound to it
- A **MAC address** (for Ethernet interfaces)

The four `ip` objects map directly to the four layers of information you need to manage:

| Object | What it controls | Common verbs |
|--------|-----------------|--------------|
| `ip link` | Interface state and flags | `show`, `set up`, `set down` |
| `ip addr` | IP addresses bound to interfaces | `show`, `add`, `del` |
| `ip route` | Routing table entries | `show`, `add`, `del`, `get` |
| `ip neigh` | ARP / neighbour cache | `show`, `flush` |

## Part 2: Exploring Your VM's Current Network

Before setting up any lab environment, take a few minutes to examine the real network configuration of your VM. This grounds everything that follows in something tangible — you will see exactly the kind of output the `ip` command produces, on a live and working network stack.

### Step 1: Identify Your Network Interface

```bash
ip link show
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/7549ac1f4b11cc59ba30c571a184bc22b28fce46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2015/images/image.png)

In the Poridhi lab environment you will see more interfaces than just `lo` and `eth0`. Here is what each one is:

| Interface | What it is | Relevant to this lab? |
|-----------|------------|-----------------------|
| `lo` | Loopback — used for local process communication | No |
| `bond0` | Network bonding interface — aggregates physical NICs for redundancy or throughput; DOWN in this environment | No |
| `dummy0` | Software dummy interface — a no-op virtual device used by the platform for internal routing; DOWN | No |
| `eth0` | **Your primary interface — this is carrying your SSH session** | Read-only observation only |
| `wt0` | WireGuard VPN tunnel — the Poridhi platform uses this for connectivity between VMs | No |
| `docker0` | Docker's bridge interface — present because Docker is installed; DOWN means no containers are currently running | No |

Your SSH connection runs over **`eth0`**. Everything else is either DOWN or managed by the platform. The only interfaces you will touch in this lab are `veth-host` (created in Part 3) and `veth-ns` (which lives inside the namespace).

The output format for each entry is:

```
<index>: <name>: <flags> mtu <mtu> ...
    link/<type> <mac-address> brd <broadcast-mac>
```

Key flags to recognise:

| Flag | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `UP` | Interface is administratively enabled |
| `LOWER_UP` | Physical or virtual link is detected (carrier present) |
| `NO-CARRIER` | Interface is up but no physical link detected |
| `BROADCAST` | Interface supports broadcast (standard Ethernet) |
| `LOOPBACK` | Interface is the loopback |
| `MULTICAST` | Interface supports multicast |
| `POINTOPOINT` | Point-to-point link with no broadcast — typical for VPN tunnels like `wt0` |

### Step 2: Check Your VM's IP Address

```bash
ip addr show
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/7549ac1f4b11cc59ba30c571a184bc22b28fce46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2015/images/image-1.png)

Look at the `inet` line under `eth0`. It will show your VM's IP address and subnet prefix — for example:

```
inet 10.0.1.15/16 brd 10.0.1.255 scope global eth0
```

### Step 3: View Your VM's Routing Table

```bash
ip route show
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/7549ac1f4b11cc59ba30c571a184bc22b28fce46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2015/images/image-2.png)

You will see at least two entries: a directly connected route for your subnet (e.g., `10.0.1.0/16 dev eth0 ...`) and a default route pointing to your gateway (e.g., `default via 10.0.1.1 dev eth0`). This is a real, working routing table — exactly what you will be creating from scratch inside the namespace shortly.

> **Note:** Do not modify any of these entries. These are the routes keeping your SSH connection alive. All practice changes in this lab happen inside an isolated namespace.

## Part 3: Setting Up the Lab Environment

We will create a **virtual Ethernet pair** (veth) inside a network namespace. A veth pair is like a virtual cable with two ends — one end lives inside the namespace (representing app-01), the other stays on the host (representing the gateway).

### Step 1: Create a Network Namespace

```bash
sudo ip netns add lab-net
```

Verify it was created:

```bash
ip netns list
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/7549ac1f4b11cc59ba30c571a184bc22b28fce46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2015/images/image-3.png)

A new namespace starts with only a loopback interface in `DOWN` state — no addresses, no routes, completely isolated.

### Step 2: Create a Virtual Ethernet Pair

```bash
sudo ip link add veth-host type veth peer name veth-ns
```

This single command creates two linked virtual interfaces: `veth-host` stays on the host, `veth-ns` will be moved into the namespace.

```bash
ip link show type veth
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/7549ac1f4b11cc59ba30c571a184bc22b28fce46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2015/images/image-4.png)

Both ends appear on the host for now, both in `DOWN` state.

### Step 3: Move One End into the Namespace

```bash
sudo ip link set veth-ns netns lab-net
```

Now `veth-ns` only exists inside `lab-net` and disappears from the host's interface list. Verify:

```bash
ip link show type veth
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/7549ac1f4b11cc59ba30c571a184bc22b28fce46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2015/images/image-5.png)

Only `veth-host` remains visible on the host. To run any command inside the namespace, prefix it with `sudo ip netns exec lab-net`:

```bash
sudo ip netns exec lab-net ip link show
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/7549ac1f4b11cc59ba30c571a184bc22b28fce46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2015/images/image-6.png)

You will see `lo` and `veth-ns` — both in `DOWN` state. This is our isolated app-01.

## Part 4: Managing Interfaces with `ip link`

### Step 1: Bring an Interface Up

Both ends of the veth pair must be `UP` for traffic to flow. Bring up the host side first:

```bash
sudo ip link set veth-host up
ip link show veth-host
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/7549ac1f4b11cc59ba30c571a184bc22b28fce46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2015/images/image-7.png)

Now bring up both interfaces inside the namespace:

```bash
sudo ip netns exec lab-net ip link set lo up
sudo ip netns exec lab-net ip link set veth-ns up
sudo ip netns exec lab-net ip link show
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/7549ac1f4b11cc59ba30c571a184bc22b28fce46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2015/images/image-8.png)

Both interfaces now show `UP, LOWER_UP` — the link is live end-to-end.

> **Warning:** `veth-host` is a virtual interface created specifically for this lab — it carries no live traffic and is completely safe to modify. Your primary interface (`eth0`) is different: it is carrying your active SSH connection. Never run `sudo ip link set eth0 down` directly on the host — it will immediately terminate your SSH session with no recovery path except restarting the VM.

## Part 5: Managing IP Addresses with `ip addr`

### Step 1: View Assigned Addresses

`ip addr show` (shorthand: `ip a`) lists every interface with all bound addresses:

```bash
# Show all interfaces and their addresses on the host
ip addr show

# Show only veth-host
ip addr show veth-host
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/7549ac1f4b11cc59ba30c571a184bc22b28fce46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2015/images/image-9.png)

Reading the address output:

```
2: eth0: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 1500 ...
    inet 10.0.1.15/24 brd 10.0.1.255 scope global eth0
       valid_lft forever preferred_lft forever
    inet6 fe80::...
```

| Field | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| `inet` | IPv4 address with CIDR prefix length |
| `inet6` | IPv6 address |
| `brd` | Broadcast address derived from the prefix |
| `scope global` | Address is globally routable |
| `scope link` | Address is only valid on the directly attached link (link-local) |
| `valid_lft forever` | Address has no expiry (static); DHCP leases show a countdown |

### Step 2: Assign the Primary IP

Assign `10.10.0.100/24` to the namespace interface (app-01's address) and `10.10.0.1/24` to the host end (the gateway):

```bash
sudo ip netns exec lab-net ip addr add 10.10.0.100/24 dev veth-ns
sudo ip netns exec lab-net ip addr show veth-ns
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/7549ac1f4b11cc59ba30c571a184bc22b28fce46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2015/images/image-10.png)

```bash
sudo ip addr add 10.10.0.1/24 dev veth-host
ip addr show veth-host
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/7549ac1f4b11cc59ba30c571a184bc22b28fce46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2015/images/image-11.png)

### Step 3: Test Connectivity

```bash
sudo ip netns exec lab-net ping -c 3 10.10.0.1
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/7549ac1f4b11cc59ba30c571a184bc22b28fce46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2015/images/image-12.png)

Three successful replies confirm the interface is up, the addresses are assigned, and the kernel's directly-connected route is working.

### Step 4: Add a Secondary IP Address

Linux allows multiple IP addresses on a single interface. This is used for hosting multiple environments, virtual IPs for load balancers, or alias addresses for services:

```bash
sudo ip netns exec lab-net ip addr add 10.10.0.200/24 dev veth-ns
sudo ip netns exec lab-net ip addr show veth-ns
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/7549ac1f4b11cc59ba30c571a184bc22b28fce46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2015/images/image-13.png)

Both `10.10.0.100` and `10.10.0.200` are now bound to `veth-ns`. Verify both are reachable from the host:

```bash
sudo ping -c 2 10.10.0.100
sudo ping -c 2 10.10.0.200
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/7549ac1f4b11cc59ba30c571a184bc22b28fce46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2015/images/image-14.png)

### Step 5: Remove an IP Address

```bash
sudo ip netns exec lab-net ip addr del 10.10.0.200/24 dev veth-ns
sudo ip netns exec lab-net ip addr show veth-ns
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/7549ac1f4b11cc59ba30c571a184bc22b28fce46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2015/images/image-15.png)

The secondary address is gone. The primary remains unaffected.

**Why it matters**: Adding and removing addresses without touching the interface or restarting services is essential for zero-downtime operations — rotating IPs during a deployment, adding a virtual IP for a failover cluster, or cleanly removing a deprecated address from a decommissioned service.

## Part 6: Routing with `ip route`

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/7549ac1f4b11cc59ba30c571a184bc22b28fce46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2015/images/routing-decision.svg)

The **routing table** tells the kernel: "When a packet is destined for network X, send it out via interface Y, optionally through gateway Z." Every packet the kernel forwards is matched against this table from most specific (longest prefix) to least specific (default route).

### Step 1: View the Routing Table

```bash
# Host routing table
ip route show

# Namespace routing table
sudo ip netns exec lab-net ip route show
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/7549ac1f4b11cc59ba30c571a184bc22b28fce46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2015/images/image-16.png)

Understanding a routing table entry:

```
10.10.0.0/24 dev veth-host proto kernel scope link src 10.10.0.1
```

| Field | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| `10.10.0.0/24` | Destination network this entry matches |
| `dev veth-host` | Send matching packets out this interface |
| `proto kernel` | Route was added automatically when the IP address was assigned |
| `scope link` | Destination is on a directly attached link — no gateway needed |
| `src 10.10.0.1` | Use this address as the source IP when originating traffic |

A **default route** looks like:

```
default via 192.168.1.1 dev eth0
```

This matches any destination not covered by a more specific entry — it is the "send everything else here" rule. Without it, the host can only reach directly connected subnets.

### Step 2: Add a Static Route

The database subnet `10.20.0.0/24` is not directly connected to app-01. Traffic to it must be forwarded via `10.10.0.1` — the host end of the veth pair. Add this route inside the namespace:

```bash
sudo ip netns exec lab-net ip route add 10.20.0.0/24 via 10.10.0.1
sudo ip netns exec lab-net ip route show
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/7549ac1f4b11cc59ba30c571a184bc22b28fce46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2015/images/image-17.png)

The new entry `10.20.0.0/24 via 10.10.0.1 dev veth-ns` now appears. Any packet destined for the database subnet will be handed to `10.10.0.1` (the host side) for forwarding.

> **Note:** In this lab, `10.10.0.1` is the IP we assigned to `veth-host` on the host. It acts as the next-hop from the namespace's perspective. In a real deployment, this address would belong to an actual upstream router with its own routing table and internet connectivity — here it simply represents where the namespace sends traffic it cannot deliver directly.

### Step 3: Set the Default Gateway

Without a default route, app-01 cannot reach anything outside of `10.10.0.0/24`:

```bash
sudo ip netns exec lab-net ip route add default via 10.10.0.1
sudo ip netns exec lab-net ip route show
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/7549ac1f4b11cc59ba30c571a184bc22b28fce46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2015/images/image-18.png)

The routing table now has three entries: the directly connected `10.10.0.0/24`, the static route to `10.20.0.0/24`, and the default gateway for everything else.

### Step 4: Trace a Routing Decision with `ip route get`

`ip route get` performs a kernel routing lookup for a specific destination and shows the exact entry that will be used — including which source IP and interface the packet will leave from. No actual traffic is sent:

```bash
# Which route handles traffic to the database subnet?
# 10.20.0.5 is a hypothetical host inside that subnet — it does not need to exist.
# ip route get only performs a lookup; no packet is ever sent.
sudo ip netns exec lab-net ip route get 10.20.0.5

# Which route handles external traffic?
sudo ip netns exec lab-net ip route get 8.8.8.8

# Which route handles traffic to the gateway itself?
sudo ip netns exec lab-net ip route get 10.10.0.1
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/7549ac1f4b11cc59ba30c571a184bc22b28fce46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2015/images/image-19.png)

`ip route get` only performs a kernel routing table lookup — it never sends a packet and does not require the destination to be a real, reachable host. You can use any address in the subnet you want to test. This makes it the definitive answer to "why is my traffic taking the wrong path?" — it shows the exact kernel decision without any ambiguity.

### Step 5: Delete a Route

```bash
sudo ip netns exec lab-net ip route del 10.20.0.0/24
sudo ip netns exec lab-net ip route show
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/7549ac1f4b11cc59ba30c571a184bc22b28fce46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2015/images/image-20.png)

The static route is gone. Only the directly connected route and the default gateway remain.

**Why it matters**: Static routes are essential in environments where you need precise control over traffic paths — microservice clusters, VPN gateways, and multi-homed servers with separate public and private interfaces. An incorrect routing table causes packets to leave from the wrong interface or not be sent at all.

## Part 7: Inspecting the ARP / Neighbour Cache

When the kernel needs to send a packet to a host on a directly connected subnet, it first needs the MAC address for that IP. This mapping is stored in the **ARP cache** (also called the neighbour table):

```bash
# After pinging, check the ARP cache on the host
ip neigh show
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/7549ac1f4b11cc59ba30c571a184bc22b28fce46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2015/images/image-21.png)

Each entry shows: `<IP> dev <interface> lladdr <MAC> <state>`

| State | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| `REACHABLE` | Entry is fresh — ARP reply was received recently |
| `STALE` | Entry has not been confirmed recently but may still be valid |
| `DELAY` | About to probe to confirm if entry is still valid |
| `FAILED` | ARP probe was sent but no reply — host is unreachable or IP is wrong |

```bash
# Clear stale entries to force fresh ARP resolution
sudo ip neigh flush dev veth-host
ip neigh show dev veth-host
```

**Why it matters**: ARP issues cause mysterious connectivity failures between hosts on the same subnet even when routing is correct. A `FAILED` neighbour entry means the kernel tried to resolve a MAC address and got no reply — indicating a dead host, an incorrect IP, or a firewall blocking ARP. `ip neigh flush` forces re-resolution and is often the fix for "I can ping the gateway but not my neighbour" problems.


## Conclusion

In this lab, we used the `ip` command to manage every layer of the Linux networking stack from a single, consistent interface:

- `ip link` controls whether an interface is active — bringing it up or down and observing its state and flags
- `ip addr` binds and removes IP addresses — multiple addresses per interface are fully supported
- `ip route` controls the routing table, mapping destination networks to interfaces and gateways
- `ip neigh` exposes the ARP cache — the bridge between IP addresses and hardware MAC addresses
- `ip route get` answers the question "which path will this packet take?" without sending any traffic

These four objects cover the complete daily networking workflow for a Linux administrator: configuring a new server, adding a failover IP, adjusting routing paths, and diagnosing why traffic is flowing through the wrong interface. The `ip` command replaced `ifconfig` and `route` because it is more consistent, more precise, and handles modern Linux networking features — including namespaces, policy routing, and multiple routing tables — that the older tools never supported.
